title: How the Brain Processes Information to Make Decisions - Reflective and Reactive Systems

segments.title: Reactive decision-making
segments.script: The human brain processes information for decision-making using one of two routes: a reflective system and a reactive (or reflexive) system. The reflective system is logical, analytical, deliberate, and methodical, while the reactive system is quick, impulsive, and intuitive, relying on emotions or habits to provide cues for what to do next. Research in neuropsychology suggests that the brain can only use one system at a time for processing information [Darlow & Sloman] and that the two systems are directed by different parts of the brain. The prefrontal cortex is more involved in the reflective system, and the basal ganglia and amygdala (more primitive parts of the brain, from an evolutionary perspective) are more involved in the reactive system. We tend to assume that the logical, analytical route leads to superior decisions, but whether this is accurate depends on the situation. The quick, intuitive route can be lifesaving; when we suddenly feel intense fear, a fight-or-flight response kicks in that leads to immediate action without methodically weighing all possible options and their consequences. Additionally, experienced managers can often make decisions very quickly because experience or expertise has taught them what to do in a given situation. These managers might not be able to explain the logic behind their decision, and will instead say they just went with their "gut," or did what "felt" right. Because the manager has faced a similar situation in the past and has figured out how to deal with it, the brain shifts immediately to the quick, intuitive decision-making system.
keyPoints: The brain uses one of two routes for decisions: a reflective system and a reactive, or reflexive, system
The reflective system is logical, analytical, deliberate and methodical; the reactive system is quick, impulsive and intuitive
The prefrontal cortex drives the reflective system, while the basal ganglia and amygdala drive the reactive system
The quick, reactive route can be lifesaving in fear responses, and lets experienced managers act fast on developed expertise
segments.altExplanation: The brain has two separate ways to decide, and it only runs one at a time. One is slow and careful, the other fast and gut-driven. Neither is automatically the better route: a fast, experience-based call can beat a slow one, especially when the situation is familiar.
segments.deeper: The reflective and reactive systems map onto different brain regions: the prefrontal cortex for reflective, deliberate thought, and the more evolutionarily primitive basal ganglia and amygdala for reactive, emotion- or habit-driven responses. This is why an experienced manager's fast 'gut' call is not guesswork: it is the reactive system applying a pattern the brain has already learned from a similar past situation.

checkpoint.prompt: Explain the two systems used by the brain in decision-making.
checkpoint.answer: The brain processes information to make decisions using one of two systems: either the logical, rational (reflective) system or the quick, reactive system. The reflective system is better for significant and important decisions; these generally should not be rushed. However, the reactive system can be lifesaving when time is of the essence, and it can be much more efficient when based on developed experience and expertise.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name both systems (reflective: logical, analytical, better for significant decisions; reactive: quick, intuitive, useful when speed matters or when based on experience) and give at least one reason each is used.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can experienced managers often make fast decisions without being able to explain their logic?
options: Experience lets the brain shift to quick, intuitive processing
They consult multiple stakeholders before deciding
They rely on emotional intelligence to read stakeholders
They follow a fixed, step-by-step decision procedure
checkpoint.answer: Experience lets the brain shift to quick, intuitive processing
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about experience or expertise letting the brain shift straight to the quick, intuitive (reactive) system.

segments.title: Reflective decision-making
segments.script: The quick route is not always the best decision-making path to take, however. When faced with novel and complex situations, it is better to process available information logically, analytically, and methodically. As a manager, you need to think about whether a situation requires not a fast, "gut" reaction, but some serious thought prior to making a decision. It is especially important to pay attention to your emotions, because strong emotions can make it difficult to process information rationally. Successful managers recognize the effects of emotions and know to wait and address a volatile situation after their emotions have calmed down. Intense emotions, whether positive or negative, tend to pull us toward the quick, reactive route of decision making. Have you ever made a large "impulse" purchase that you were excited about, only to regret it later? This speaks to the power our emotions exert on our decision-making. Big decisions should generally not be made impulsively, but reflectively.
keyPoints: Novel and complex situations call for logical, analytical, methodical processing rather than a fast gut reaction
Strong emotions, positive or negative, make it harder to process information rationally
Successful managers wait and address a volatile situation only after their emotions have calmed down
Intense emotions pull us toward the quick, reactive route, so big decisions should be made reflectively, not impulsively
segments.altExplanation: Some decisions deserve the slow route: work through the situation logically instead of trusting the first gut feeling. That matters most when emotions are running high, because strong feelings, good or bad, pull us toward acting fast rather than thinking it through.
segments.deeper: The passage's impulse-purchase example shows how the reactive route can misfire even outside high-stakes management decisions: strong emotion, not the size of the decision, is what pulls us toward acting quickly. The practical rule that follows is to notice the emotional intensity of a situation and deliberately delay big or novel decisions until that intensity has passed.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the book say big decisions should be made reflectively rather than impulsively?
checkpoint.answer: Because intense emotions, whether positive or negative, tend to pull us toward the quick, reactive route, and acting on that impulse can lead to choices we later regret, like an impulse purchase. Novel and complex situations instead call for processing information logically, analytically, and methodically.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say strong emotion pulls decision-making toward the fast, reactive route with a risk of regret, and that novel or complex situations need logical, methodical (reflective) processing instead.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, when is the quick, gut reaction not the best path to take?
options: When the decision affects only individual outcomes
When situations are novel and complex
When a manager has already faced a similar situation
When stakeholders have no stake in the outcome
checkpoint.answer: When situations are novel and complex
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option naming novel and complex situations as calling for reflective rather than quick, gut decision-making.

segments.title: Emotions and emotional intelligence
segments.script: Being aware of the role emotions play in decision-making does not mean that we should ignore them. Emotions can serve as powerful signals about what we should do, especially in situations with ethical implications. You can read more about this particular type of decision-making in the Ethics in Practice box later in this chapter. Thinking through how we feel about the possible options, and why we feel that way, can greatly enhance our decision-making. Effective decision-making, then, relies on both logic and emotions. For this reason, the concept of emotional intelligence has become popular as a characteristic of effective managers. Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, pay attention to, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others. It involves self-awareness and self-regulation, essentially, this is a toggling back and forth between emotions and logic so that we analyze and understand our own emotions and then exert the necessary control to manage them as appropriate for the situation. Emotional intelligence also involves empathy, the ability to understand other peoples' emotions (and an interest in doing so). Finally, emotional intelligence involves social skills to manage the emotional aspects of relationships with others. Managers who are aware of their own emotions can think through what their emotions mean in a given situation and use that information to guide their decision-making. Managers who are aware of the emotions of others can also utilize that information to help groups function more effectively and engage in better group decision-making. While emotional intelligence seems to come easily to some people, it is something that we can develop and improve on with practice.
keyPoints: Being aware of emotions in decision-making does not mean ignoring them; emotions can be powerful signals, especially in ethical situations
Effective decision-making relies on both logic and emotion, which is why emotional intelligence matters for managers
Emotional intelligence is recognizing, understanding, attending to and managing one's own emotions and other people's emotions
It involves self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social skills, and can be developed and improved with practice
segments.altExplanation: Emotions are not the enemy of good decisions; they are information. The skill is noticing what you and others feel, understanding why, and then using logic to decide what to do about it. That back-and-forth between feeling and reasoning is what the book calls emotional intelligence.
segments.deeper: The passage lists four components of emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, and social skills, framed as a toggling between emotion and logic rather than a replacement of one by the other. Because it can be developed with practice, it is treated as a learnable managerial skill rather than a fixed trait, which is why it comes up repeatedly as a way managers can offset bias and improve group decision-making.

checkpoint.prompt: What does emotional intelligence involve, according to the passage?
options: Following a fixed, programmed decision procedure
Weighing outcomes across every stakeholder group
Recognizing and managing one's own and others' emotions
Reacting quickly based on gut instinct alone
checkpoint.answer: Recognizing and managing one's own and others' emotions
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about recognizing, understanding and managing one's own and other people's emotions.

checkpoint.prompt: What is emotional intelligence, and why is it important for decision-making?
checkpoint.answer: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, pay attention to, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others, involving self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, and social skills. It matters for decision-making because effective decisions rely on both logic and emotion, so understanding how and why we feel can improve decisions we make alone or in groups.
checkpoint.rubric: Must define emotional intelligence as recognizing, understanding or managing one's own and others' emotions (naming at least one of self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy or social skills), and connect it to decision-making relying on both logic and emotion.
